title: Ayyub called out
hookLine: the Quran's Job, patient in affliction, calls to God and is answered
last: HIS EYES GO WHITE WITH GRIEF.

lines: JOB HAS A NAME IN THE QURAN.
cards: Some people will carry a heavy box up the stairs, arms shaking, rather than ask the neighbor on the landing to grab one end.
For them, asking can look like failing, as if patience means silence, and silence means strength. Not long ago, this path met Job in the Bible: the good man who lost everything and argued with God.
The Quran knows him too, and calls him Ayyub. And the Quran, which praises his patience, also remembers the moment he opened his mouth and asked.

teach.h: JOB IS AYYUB IN THE QURAN.
teach.b: First, who he is. The Quran tells Ayyub's story in short passages. It doesn't stage long debates with friends.
It gives his affliction, his prayer, and the answer. Second, the call.

teach.h: HARM HAS TOUCHED ME. YOU ARE MERCIFUL.
teach.b: In the chapter of the Prophets, Ayyub cries out to his Lord: harm has touched me, and you are the most merciful of those who show mercy. That's all. He doesn't demand a reason, and he doesn't hide the pain.
He says two true things side by side: this hurts, and you are merciful. Third, the answer.
The very next verse says God answered him, removed the harm, and gave him back his family and as many again with them, a mercy, and a reminder for those who worship.
In another chapter, the answer is physical: strike the ground with your foot, and there is cool water, to wash in and to drink. Fourth, the surprise.
In that same passage, after the call and the healing, God says: We found him patient. How excellent a servant.
The man who called out is the one the Quran calls patient. In this telling, asking isn't the opposite of patience. Sabr holds steady; it doesn't mean pretending to be fine.
The Bible's Job argues; the Quran's Ayyub calls. Each book remembers him its own way, and neither has him stay silent.

how: Some Muslims recite Ayyub's words from Quran 21:83 as a supplication in illness and hardship, and his story is told as an example of patience that still turns to God for help.

practice: Choose one thing you're carrying alone that you don't have to, and trim it down to one plain sentence, no backstory, no apology: this is hard for me.
If you can, say it out loud, even in a whisper, and notice what it's like to hear it in your own voice. If you pray, you can call out to God the way Ayyub did.
